newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Aussie dlr back to daily drudge after grey budget.
newsitem.headline: Aussie dlr back to daily drudge after grey budget.

text.p: The Australian dollar settled into all too familiar range trading Wednesday as the market put the disappointment of the budget behind it only to find fundamentals offered little direction either.
The currency suffered early nerves as the government tried to portray the budget as a force for lower interest rates, and tested US$0.7760 support for a while.

Most analysts, however, reckoned the Reserve Bank would be just as deflated by the lack of real spending cuts as the market and the easing talk found few takers. The dollar enjoyed support as a result and looked set to orbit 78 cents for a while yet.
By 5.00 pm (0700 GMT) the dollar found itself back at US$0.7782/87 after opening at US$0.7760/65 having retreated from the US$0.7826/31 level held just before the budget.
This was well within the US$0.7720/7860 range which has contained the currency since early April and left technical indicators flat and uninspiring.

The deadlock also spawned rumours that some well known speculators from Asia and the U.S. were defending big strangle options plays and traders did spot sizeable selling out of the Chicago IMM futures pit overnight when the currency was threatening to break US$0.7835 resistance.
Such talk was more a symptom of the range trading malaise than a cause but did serve to make dealers ever more cautious about taking positions.
Which was why many had hoped the 1997/98 budget would end the stalemate and why they were so disappointed by the thin, unexciting offering from the government.

"It was a pretty pitiful effort," said John Kyriakopoulos, an economist at J.P. Morgan Australia, whoi felt the reliance on cyclical forces to deliver an eventual surplus was a mistake. The lack of additional fiscal tightening also made it harder for the RBA to ease, no matter what government rhetoric claimed.

"Insofar as there is a trade-off between fiscal and monetary policy, the budget has left no room for a rate cut," he said. "From that point of view it will be very interesting to see if Macfarlane says anything about the budget tomorrow."
RBA governor Ian Macfarlane gives an address on monetary policy to the Jewish Chamber of Commerce at lunchtime Thursday.
Only last week Macfarlane ruled out an easing for the foreseeable future saying he saw no economic benefit in a move.
If he repeated that line, it should help cushion the dollar at a time when its interest advantage was under threat from developments in both the U.S. and Japan.
In the U.S. the market remains divided on whether the Federal Reserve will tighten policy again at its May 20 meeting but a 25 basis point rise would certainly be no surprise.
Data on U.S. producer prices tonight and consumer prices Thursday may help crystalise market thinking and could end up having more impact on the local dollar than domestic events.

In contrast analysts thought the risk of a near term hike in Japanese rates was being greatly overstated and pointed to jitters in Japan's financial system today as just one reason for the BOJ to hang fire. This time the rumours of a bank in trouble proved wide of the mark, but most felt it only a matter of time.

The yen wavered on the talk and the dollar crept up to 92.57/67 yen from an early 91.74 low, but was still short of Tuesday's late 93.20/30. In trade weighted terms the currency was down at 59.5 from a previous 59.9 finish.
The market's subdued respoinse to the budget was echoed by the major ratings agencies with both S&P and Moody's saying the budget alone was not enough to trigger a credit upgrade.
Longer term, analysts were somewhat mollified that the budget was projected to reach an underlying surplus in 1998/99 and beyond, a performance unmatched by most OECD countries.
